Alright, the current situation: I've just kicked off a full end‑to‑end training pipeline test (`test_full_pipeline_end_to_end`) in the background using the `byclyremo` task. The command is running with a fairly generous timeout (250 s) and will produce a lot of console output, including the various stages of the STM (Sparse Transformer Module) training loop. I need to keep an eye on its progress so I can react appropriately—especially to know when it reaches the STM phase, when it finishes (passes), or if it crashes (fails or errors).

I already have a background task ID (`byclyremo`) and its output is being written to `/tmp/claude-1000/-home-lane-MythosMini/602033e7-dc55-4b7f-909f-1c67135d8f4b/tasks/byclyremo.output`. The simplest way to monitor this is to poll the file until I see a line that signals a major milestone. The markers I care about are:

- `"stm phase"` – indicates the start of the STM training loop.
- `"passed"` – indicates the test succeeded.
- `"failed"` – indicates the test failed.
- `"Error"` – any unexpected exception.

I could just `tail -f` the file, but that would block indefinitely and I wouldn't be able to continue other work. Instead, I can use a non‑blocking loop: repeatedly `grep` the output file for any of those keywords, sleeping a few seconds between attempts. Once a match is found, I can break out of the loop and then `tail` the last few lines to give a concise summary of what just happened, stripping out any progress bars (`%` characters) that clutter the output.

Because I want this monitoring to happen concurrently with the rest of my workflow, I should run the whole waiting command in the background as well. That way, the assistant can continue issuing other commands (e.g., profiling, linting) while this monitor silently watches the test. The command will be:

```
until grep -qE "stm phase|passed|failed|Error" /tmp/.../byclyremo.output 2>/dev/null; do sleep 5; done;
tail -20 /tmp/.../byclyremo.output | grep -v "%|"
```

The `until` loop will exit as soon as any of the patterns appear. After exiting, `tail -20` will fetch the most recent 20 lines (enough to capture context around the marker) and the final `grep -v "%|"` will filter out any lines containing `%` or `|`, which are typical of progress bar output from `tqdm` or similar.

Now I need to issue this as a Bash tool call, marking it to run in the background so I can keep the session responsive. The description should clearly state that I'm waiting for pipeline progress markers. This aligns with the overall goal of confirming the end‑to‑end test proceeds correctly and to surface any failures promptly.

Thus, the appropriate next action is to launch this background monitoring command.
